Issued at 1248 AM CST Sun Nov 22 2026

An upper level trough that will enter northern CA from the Pacific 
on Sunday night is progged to track east over the Great Basin and 
down to the Four Corners by Monday afternoon.  Come Monday night 
that system over the Four Corners will track over eastern NM, and 
this is where the location of the system will be critical.  Overall 
this system is expected to have a deep moisture profile which is 
normally a challenge when you take the system across the interior 
CONUS, and a lot of that moisture can be pulled out over the 
Rockies as well as when colliding with other areas of drier air. 
But there is a little wave of 700mb moisture late Sunday night 
that is coming in off the eastern Pacific that's progged to track 
due north and collide with the remaining moisture from the upper 
level trough right over the eastern NM area and the Panhandles. 
Model soundings out ahead of the trough all show very deep 
moisture profiles with ample lift ahead of the profiles. They also
show lapse rates that are getting close to that 6.0-6.5C range in
the 700-500mb layer. Given the dynamic tropopause fold setup and 
the potential for models to underplay slightly colder air aloft, 
the current setup is more of a slantwise convective setup. If 
lapse rates can steepen a bit more then we could have more 
vertical growth, which could even lead to some isolated 
thundersnow. This overall setup is very much favoring an area of 
snow bands that would be scattered from eastern NM to south of the
Panhandles, and may even be over the Panhandles. This also makes 
forecasting the location of the snow very difficult as every 
single model update will move where one of the bands is located, 
and just how much snow will come out of it. Some have noted 
bullseye of 4-6 inches (this is over a very small area, about the 
size of a small city) where just a couple miles north or south of 
that bullseye you will find maybe an inch, then a little further 
away nothing. This also lines up with why the NBM is struggling 
with any probabilities of an inch because there's too much 
diversity in the models as to where they want the bands to end up,
but the overall probability of measurable snow for the western 
and southern Panhandles manage to range from 30-70% because of all
the various locations of these snow bands. The highest confidence
in this system (at this time) looks to be that we will be cold 
enough for snow. Most of the cluster ensembles that have 
precipitation, has it as snow. It's really just nailing down where
these snow bands will occur. While there is certainly the 
possibility of 1 to multiple bands of snow in the western to 
southern Panhandle (Amarillo included), a big failure potential is
the drier air from the east eroding out the moisture and shutting
down the snow. This will not be for all areas, but if it happens 
for the Panhandles that increases the probability that this will 
all occur west in NM and south of highway 287. Latest GFS model is
pulling more moisture in the Panhandles all the way to the OK 
border, but RRFS is taking the drier route and barely any snow for
the southwest Panhandles. Watching where this dry air stalls out 
is key. Another thing to always watch is that shortwave, it could 
track further north or south and that changes the location and 
impacts. Overall, whatever snow bands that do occur, should take 
place very late Monday night and be done by Tuesday early 
afternoon. Lastly, if we do manage to pick up snow, something to 
watch for Tuesday night would be any roads that remain wet. Lows
will be in the mid 20s, so if the roads are not treated ice could
form on the surface. 

Late Tuesday afternoon through Saturday Night.  A break from active 
weather as we transition to a cool northerly flow on the back side 
of the departing trough.  This will be followed by a more mild split 
flow on Thursday night due to another weather system diving down 
over NM and down by the Baja.  Then by Friday and Saturday we turn 
more mild as high pressure over the western CONUS builds and we get 
a more mild dry northwest flow over the Panhandles.  So much that we 
look to get back into the 50s.  

Weber
